entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Igor Fyodorovich Stravinsky (1882–1971) was a Russian-born composer whose 'The Rite of Spring' (1913) provoked a riot at its Paris premiere and launched the modernist revolution in music. Across seven decades, he reinvented his style three times—from Russian nationalism to neoclassicism to serialism—making him the most influential composer of the 20th century.

Born near St. Petersburg and trained under Rimsky-Korsakov, Stravinsky achieved fame with three ballets for Diaghilev's Ballets Russes: 'The Firebird' (1910), 'Petrushka' (1911), and 'The Rite of Spring' (1913). The Rite's savage rhythms, polytonal harmonies, and primitivist choreography were so shocking that the audience erupted in fistfights on opening night.

After World War I, Stravinsky pivoted to neoclassicism—drawing on Bach, Pergolesi, and Mozart in works like 'Pulcinella' (1920) and 'Symphony of Psalms' (1930). After 1950, he astonished the music world again by adopting the twelve-tone serial techniques of his former rival Schoenberg.

Stravinsky lived in Switzerland, France, and finally Los Angeles, becoming a US citizen in 1945. His total output—ballets, symphonies, concertos, operas, and sacred music—reshaped every dimension of musical composition. As he declared: 'I have learned throughout my life that the important thing is not what one likes or dislikes, but what one can renounce.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Stravinsky's 'The Rite of Spring' (1913) revolutionized modern music, influencing generations of composers and shaping the course of 20th-century classical music. Its impact can be measured by the lasting influence on musical styles, with over 100 compositions directly inspired by its innovative techniques.
